column2: Alice, a former student, and several women students in leather jackets used to hop freight trains to New York during vacations; once arrested by the railroad police, they had to wait for a faculty member to make a long trip to pay their fines. Leather jackets; fines paid by a teacher; the creation of one of the few rules: students must not hop freight trains Consequences: One of the college's very few rules: a ban on hopping freight trains.

After leaving the college, Alice and some friends sawed off the angel at the top of the steeple of an old church in lower Manhattan, took it to San Francisco, and, when they opened a lesbian bar on the Embarcadero waterfront in the 1950s, hung it over the door and named the place The Tin Angel. Hacksaw; tin angel; waterfront lesbian bar

Tommy annoyed the administration: breaking the padlocks on the food cupboards (put there because of his raids), sending out printed poems as if they bore the college's imprimatur, which especially drew Olson's anger; after the quarrel he renamed his press from Grapnel Press to Terrified Press, becoming a nonconformist among nonconformists. Forced padlocks; printed poems; new name: The Terrified Press Consequences: Tommy marginalized within the college itself.
Dorothy and Pat, school friends; Pat constantly praised her brilliant friend and persuaded her to come and try Black Mountain. Consequences: The beginning of the Tommy–Dorothy romance.

Birds would come in through the metal stovepipe, fall into the cold stove, escape through the stove door, and beat against the wall of glass; one morning Rumaker opened the door to let them out. Potbellied stove; wall of glass

In the college's last years, Nell Rice, sidelined first by John Rice and then under the Olson regime, becomes a vengeful woman and helps, with Natasha Goldowski and Johanna Jalowetz (another recent widow living alone on campus), to bring Black Mountain down through lawsuits for back pay. Consequences: According to Rumaker, this anger contributed to the destruction of the college, which had perhaps carried the seeds of its own destruction since before its founding.

A former student (during Paul Goodman's stay), a Berkeley graduate in math and music, Glenn comes back to visit in the fall of 1952, on leave from his post as a mathematician at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where Einstein (who gave a lecture at Black Mountain in 1941) was in residence. Brush cut, chinos, a brown suede jacket; a post at Princeton Consequences: Rumaker develops a massive crush on him; long tutorial chats on the pallet in Rumaker's study.

Goodman, frighteningly uninhibited in the eyes of the college's old Quakers and Europeans, once openly urinated behind a tree during a softball game in front of the assembled college, children included: the last straw that led to his expulsion. Softball game; children present Consequences: Goodman's expulsion from the college.

On the night of the performance (only one ever, given the small campus audience), Rumaker, in pancake makeup, his hair slicked back Spanish-style, in a white shirt, black bow tie, and dark pants for the wedding day, his stomach dancing a flamenco with stage fright, plays his first scene, then, having to rush to the restroom without crossing the audience, leaves by the side door and goes up to South Lodge; applying the Black Mountain “slowdown,” he takes his time at the mirror until Wes Huss appears in the doorway, remarkably calm: “Everyone is waiting… Your next entrance was some time ago”; they run to the hall, Rumaker slips in and climbs onto his platform, the cast staring at him, Cynthia Homire severely, Bea Huss with empathetic irony. Pancake makeup, black bow tie, white shirt; a single performance per production; a run through the winter darkness Consequences: Wes tells him to save his excuses for later.

In early fall 1952, at a gathering in the hall of Meadows Inn, where Natasha Goldowski and Eric Renner live (perhaps one of Natasha's rare lectures on modern physics), Rumaker first sees the back of Merrill's head, sitting two or three rows in front of him next to his lover Herb Roco, on the universal cane-bottomed chairs lined up in the crowded hall. Seen from behind, Merrill's ears seem to him at first those of a bat, then a fawn, then a satyr: repellent fascination, a shiver. Consequences: A first impression of repulsion that precedes the attraction to come
Olson spends the fall of 1952 in Yucatán on a grant from the Wenner-Gren Foundation for Anthropological Research to study Maya glyphs.

During this period, Rauschenberg assembles: his photographs; about thirty-three collages of ephemera and old engravings rescued from secondhand booksellers and flea markets, mounted on laundry cardboards; the Scatole Personali (boxes); the Feticci Personali (fetishes) About 33 collages on laundry shirt cardboards

One September morning, two and a half years after the ritual and after saying an emotional goodbye to Franz and Nancy at the station, while brushing his teeth and shaving, Dawson, seized by sudden disgust, tears off the wart piece by piece and rubs it with his thumb: the wrist is clean. Toothbrush, razor, pieces torn off with the thumb Consequences: The end of the obsession

Dawson sits on the admissions committee (one of two students, with the admissions officer and the Business Manager); in the spring he hungrily votes “yes” for a pretty blond science girl. On a warm, cool, crisp September day, he comes out of South Lodge and sees a station wagon in front of North Lodge, tailgate down, a blonde in a white dress taking out suitcases; he helps her and introduces himself, and as she shakes his hand she says her name; he winks: he already knew it. They soon sleep together; it does not last. A glossy photograph in the file; station wagon, tailgate down, white dress, suitcases; a warm, cool, crisp September day Consequences: For months she nurses a student of Albers's who caught malaria in Mexico; she later writes to Dawson that she rides a motorcycle; a letter after the army: “You are the artist, you are the poet, you are the lover”

Dan and Fielding raise the uprights on the concrete slab (about 20 x 100 feet) with a bolted oak sill running across it; ten posts per side, four per gable end; nails toenailed in a V at the base, sighted from a distance from the pasture. Consequences: The start of exhausting work in oak

Fielding tries to start a 20-penny nail in an oak post and fails, arm, wrist, and shoulder powerless; he looks at Dan, frightened: “Dan! It just — won't — I can't get the nails in!” Dan nods: “That's oak.” Fielding throws the post to the ground and gazes at the open landscape.

Dawson holds the big post at an angle and tries to drive a 20-penny nail (a big spike) into the oak: total failure, panic. Dan nods: “That's oak.” Dawson throws down the post, contemplates the open foundation, the heavy posts, and the rough 1×5-inch boards, and realizes that the whole building has to be built with this wood. Anger at the college, too poor to buy lumber, and at Dan, who has already worked oak. 20-penny nails; rough boards 1 inch by 5; a keg of nails; Dan sweating, nailing “from his heels” Consequences: Dawson sits down, grumbling that he is no goddamn pioneer

A first post is raised, a severe and singular object. Dan goes up into the pasture and directs Dawson by voice (left… more). A nail bends; Dan comes back down and advises: it is all in the eye; fix on the nailhead, think of nothing, then strike. He puts a hand on his shoulder and adds that the barn has to be ready for the harvest. A technique for straightening a nail bent into an L with the claw of the hammer; the bend marks where it will bend again; a nail driven more than an inch into oak cannot be saved

A few days later, all the posts are up; they lay the 1×5 boards across. They climb up by a temporary board set at an angle and sit astride the unfastened board, back to back, each end resting on only two inches at the rounded top of the post. Every adjustment must be careful, or they fall. A structure of a series of H's; posts checked plumb with a spirit level: the bubble exactly between the black lines in the green liquid; they look at each other, proud: built by eye, perfect

The campus deserted, even Paul Goodman's orange dog gone; Rumaker drags his suitcase to the Studies Building, finds an open study with a bare mattress, glimpses the lake, the white heron in the reeds, the mist on the mountains; he falls asleep at once. Atmosphere: A smell of mildew, oil paint, and turpentine, the smell of Black Mountain Stakes: Arrival at the place of his possible life

Rumaker has just made the bed; the door bangs; Jorge comes in from Detroit, accosts him, learns of the room-sharing, swears at Hazel, storms off to the office, comes back inflexible: “You're movin' out”; Rumaker goes to see Hazel, who, sorry, puts him in the dormitory, his bed near the door. Words: “What the hell are you doing here?”; “That goddamned woman! She promised me…”; “You're movin' out” Atmosphere: Boxes, fury, the newcomer's incomprehension Stakes: The shy young student's baptism of fire

In the morning, a line of Black passengers (mothers, hungry children) in the corridor; empty white tables; Rumaker is seated at once, alone; a group of Black passengers penned at the only table “for colored only”; he receives his pot and silverware while the train corkscrews up toward the Swannanoa. Atmosphere: Gleaming white tablecloths, the rising sun reddening the clay of the cuts, mounting hope Stakes: An acute awareness of injustice, with the same prices for all

Bent over row after row, they cut the dead stalks and tie the bundles with twine; Terence sings “Auprès de ma blonde” and recites Villon (“Où sont les neiges d'antan”), speaks French with Don; Eric Weinberger works apart, silent and Christlike, now and then letting drop an extraordinary insight; the student from Vermont, handsome and mocking, tries to start philosophical debates and slips Rumaker coy allusions to homosexuality Words: Terence: Villon, “Où sont les neiges d'antan?” and “Auprès de ma blonde”; the student from Vermont: coy allusions to homosexuality Atmosphere: Monotonous and backbreaking until dusk; a crew of misfits, “ragtag” in “ragtag” clothes; the sudden surprise of the orange salamander with blue spots Stakes: Rumaker, 125 pounds at 6'2'' (57 kg, 1.88 m), wonders whether he will last

Single file from the farm, the stream crossed near Meadows Inn, the dirt road along the lake, a late supper kept warm; Don Jones, legs on a cane chair, jokes in his flat Middle West voice with Terence, talking painting now and then Words: Don Jones's jokes, conversations about painting Atmosphere: Deepening dusk, boiled coffee, the screen, the lake through the wire mesh; Rumaker's inner calm: “I was where I was meant to be” Stakes: Belonging, felt at last

An improvisation exercise after supper: Huss commands “Be a tree, be a reed… Be the wind”; the others throw themselves into it like atoms of air; Fee, arms folded over his faded Levi jacket, argues why he refuses to be a reed, to bend Words: Huss: “Be a tree, be a reed”; “Bend! Bend! Be the wind”; Fee: arguments against bending Atmosphere: The tension shows on Wes's face; Quaker pacifism put to the test Stakes: Teaching authority against an artist's integrity

The only one up early: eggs and grits, a mug of black coffee, a cane chair, the first Home Run of the day (a furnace in the lungs), a look at the mists on the lake, then at snowcapped Mount Mitchell Atmosphere: The college all to himself, stillness before the day, anxieties soothed by nicotine and landscape

Doyle speeds up the conveyor as he sees the sun go down; Rumaker can no longer keep up and drops his pocketknife, which disappears into the machine; a screeching halt; red with anger, Doyle jumps down from the blower and shouts; Rumaker raises his hand like a schoolboy and confesses; Doyle sends him into the silo in Fee's place; the farmers, snickering about “city boys,” pull out the bent knife and start the machine again Words: Doyle asks what happened and whether someone lost his knife, shouts that that's enough, sends him up into the silo with Ben, and orders the one up there to come down and take his place Atmosphere: The sun sinking toward the mountains, Doyle's face as red as the setting sun, the veins in his neck ready to burst, a cigarette butt on his lips Stakes: The city boy's humiliation before the farmers; Rumaker's initiation into real work

The two jump about in the silage, dancing face to face, arms spread like cranes answering each other, spiraling from the edge to the center and back to the circular wall, sliding boards into the slot; the level rises, and daylight drains from the sky; suddenly Rumaker is above the rim of the silo and sees the valley stretching away, several stories below, nausea in the pit of his stomach Atmosphere: The summery fragrance of cornstalks stinging the nostrils, dust of dead leaves raining down in a storm, amusement turning to vertigo at dusk Stakes: The intoxication of work turned to play, then the fear of the void

The silo filled to the brim, Doyle shouts to come down and cover it before it rains; Ben, nimble as a squirrel, climbs over and disappears; Rumaker, paralyzed by the same panic as on the tanker's mast, remembers the foreman's words, makes the valley his river, and climbs down one rung at a time without looking down Words: Doyle shouts to them both to come down, since they still have to cover it in case it rains Atmosphere: Thick dusk, a vast expanse of green land growing dark Stakes: A quiet triumph over fear; an echo of his father and the shipyard

After his first scene, Rumaker in his wedding costume (pancake makeup, slicked hair) leaves by the side door, goes up to the restroom at South Lodge, lingers at the mirror; Wes appears in the doorway, calm; a run back through the winter darkness; a furtive entrance, the cast staring at him. Words: Wes: everyone is waiting; is he sick? He has been looking everywhere for him; his entrance was some time ago; he tells him to save his excuses. Atmosphere: Flamenco stage fright in the stomach, contained panic, shame; Cynthia's severity, Bea's empathetic smile. Stakes: Rumaker's theatrical baptism; Wes's psychological grip.

Sitting two or three rows behind, Rumaker stares at the back of Merrill's head: in his imagination the ears turn from a bat's into a fawn's and then a satyr's; he shivers and forces himself to look away, thinking he could never be attracted to such ears Words: “I could ever be attracted to someone with ears like that,” he thinks Atmosphere: Repellent fascination, shivers Stakes: The irony of Eros the trickster: a foreshadowing of attraction

A walk beyond the barn, among cows and chickens; discovery of the slab; raising the posts, sighting from a distance; Fielding holds a post at an angle and tries to start the nail, fails despite all his arm; he looks at Dan, eyes wide and frightened; Dan nods calmly; Fielding throws down the post and stares at the landscape Words: “Dan! It just — won't — I can't get the nails in!” / “That's oak.” Atmosphere: The open sun of the pasture, the brutality of the material, physical panic Stakes: The young body confronting oak: a lesson in humility and will

Dawson holds the post at an angle, tries to start a 20-penny nail, fails, panics; throws down the post, contemplates the foundation, posts, and boards Words: “Dan! It just — won't — I can't get the nails in!” / “That's oak.” / “Do you mean — we're going to have to build this WHOLE BUILDING WITH IT?” / “It's the only wood we have.” Atmosphere: Sweat, dread, contained rage, sun on the pasture with the lake in the distance Stakes: The physical initiation into the dying college: everything still to be built with the most stubborn material

After the Dartington Hall conference, the four great ceramists agree, after long correspondence, to a ten-day session at Black Mountain, with Wildenhain serving as “host potter.” Length: ten days; the delegation arrives in mid-October; the college recovers its $800 investment thanks to special students, including local potters. Consequences: A success: many in the community who were against ceramics change their minds; a second institute takes place in the summer of 1953.

On the first day, Leach (smug and lordly) and Wildenhain declare that they will not be able to work with clays and a kiln different from their own. Hamada turns the situation around: as a painter in England, he would buy an English notebook and pencil; at Black Mountain he will use the clay and glazes at hand; the mountains remind him of Japan. Hamada picks grasses, dips them in mud, wedges the clay, throws shapes, glazes, fires, then sells a whole tray of his pieces at $2 or $3 apiece (a small Hamada pot would be worth about $300 today). He buys a pot by Leach and declares it among the best ever thrown. Consequences: The other artists set to work in turn.

Karnes and Weinrib host a ten-day pottery seminar bringing together world-famous ceramists: Shoji Hamada and Soetsu Yanagi from Japan, Bernard Leach from England, Marguerite Wildenhain from California by way of the Bauhaus. Ten days, October 1952 Consequences: Rumaker, deeply impressed, briefly tries pottery; it is mutually agreed that his talents lie more with words than with clay

A violent forest fire breaks out just after Rumaker starts in the kitchen, in the fall of 1952; at night the flames climb halfway up the slope. The forest rangers come looking for volunteers on campus and find a group in the kitchen; they pass over Rumaker, too skinny. Weinberger and Burns leave with Indian backpack pumps and red hoses and come back the next day covered in soot; Malrey has kept their food warm on the stove. “Indian Pumper” water tanks on their backs, red hoses, the smell of smoke, soot from head to toe Consequences: The fire is brought under control after a night and a day

A music student from Philadelphia, an ex-veteran, arrives at the college about a month after the start of the fall 1952 quarter, at the urging of a friend who had come earlier with his wife, both having studied composition with Stefan Wolpe in Philadelphia; he comes to resume his studies with Wolpe. Consequences: He sleeps in the attic dormitory of South Lodge and works on the farm (GI Bill)

For Barbara Fritchey's birthday, Mark writes and stages an after-dinner sketch, a silly one (“Kill if you must this old gray head but spare your country's flag!”). Wes explodes: “How dare you!”, accusing Mark of having deliberately used the space by the wooden divider, a natural backdrop he reserved for rehearsals of Mother Courage; the association would ruin his effects and diminish Brecht's seriousness. Gentle Mark, deaf and wearing a hearing aid, apologizes humbly while Wes, angrier than anyone has ever seen him, towers over him, his eyes and neck muscles bulging, his voice hoarse. Wooden divider; an after-supper sketch; Bert Morgan's home brew cited as the culture of the skits

A ceramics seminar taught by Hamada, Yanagi, and Leach, with Marguerite Wildenhain as host. The same year, an Institute in the New Sciences of Man brings together Robert Braidwood, Marie-Louise von Franz, and lectures by Olson. Consequences: Part of Olson's plan (1952) to reorganize the curriculum into institutes and eliminate the last vestiges of progressive education.

Leach, stiff and lordly, and Wildenhain declare they will not be able to work: the clays and kiln are too different. Hamada answers with a parable: as a painter in England, he would buy an English notebook and pencil; here he will use the local material; the mountains remind him of Japan. He picks grasses, dips them in mud, wedges the clay, throws, glazes, fires, then sells his pieces for $2 or $3 and buys a pot by Leach. Words: Hamada: if he were a painter in England, he would buy an English notebook and pencil; at Black Mountain he will do the same with the clay and glazes available. Atmosphere: A turning point: the institute seemed reduced to speeches and slides; Hamada's example puts everyone to work. Stakes: Saving the institute from mere talk; the rehabilitation of ceramics in the community's eyes.

After supper, for Barbara Fritchey's birthday, a silly patriotic sketch; Wes explodes and accuses Mark of sabotaging his rehearsal space for Mother Courage; gentle, deaf Mark apologizes; Wes towers over him, hoarse with anger Words: “Kill if you must this old gray head but spare your country's flag!” / “How dare you!” Atmosphere: disproportionate anger, the fear of the small one before the big one Stakes: a director's pride, violence beneath pacifism

During two weeks of demonstrations, lectures, and debates, Leach denounces American ceramics as lacking traditions; Wildenhain, an American by adoption, answers him vehemently, before publishing an open letter in Craft Horizons in 1953. Atmosphere: International erudition, notorious verbal sparring Stakes: Who has the right to define the identity of American craft?

During the seminar, Hamada gives demonstration after demonstration: he throws pots, vases, and cups in near silence on a wheel set up outdoors; the participants watch the clay rise under his hands Words: Asked about his repetition of the same motifs: “It's not the same—it is variation on sameness” Atmosphere: Contemplative silence, mastered gesture, an audience of artists from all over the country Stakes: Demonstration as performance: passing on an aesthetic through the body rather than through discourse

In the final moments of a party at the Club for Alcopley, leaving for Paris, everyone rummages through pockets and wallets to give him old bills and identity cards; Elaine takes off her right shoe and stocking and ceremoniously hands them over to applause; Nancy Ward, Kline's companion, sees a sexual message in it and takes off her bra to compete Consequences: A memorable Dada gesture

After a lecture by Bill at the museum (in which he explains in detail why he cannot draw feet, use color, compose, or finish a painting), then meals with patrons making insipid remarks, they visit the exhibition of twentieth-century sculpture and the paintings by Rubens, Ribera, and the Le Nain brothers; a rather violent argument divides them: would the composition of the beggars in rags be as strong if they wore sumptuous clothes? She says yes, he says no; yet the only Le Nain in the museum at the time, Louis Le Nain's The Reprimand, shows no beggars, a curious detail noted by the biographer Letter of late November 1952: Philadelphia has “as much to do with art as Harry Truman” Consequences: According to Jed Perl, the Le Nains are the main source of the poses, faces, colors, and moods of Bill's canvases from the late 1930s to the early 1940s

A few weeks before December, Herb Roco goes back to Houston to help his father in his auto repair shop; Merrill is seen even less since then. Consequences: Merrill finds himself alone, which precedes his approach to Rumaker

An all-night farewell party for Alcopley, leaving for Paris; everyone gives him old bills and cards; Elaine takes off her right shoe and stocking and ceremoniously hands them to him to applause; Nancy Ward, piqued, takes off her bra and offers it too Atmosphere: the feverish gaiety of the last hours of a sleepless night Stakes: a duel of gestures between women, a misunderstanding between Dada and seduction

After Thanksgiving dinner, guests pile their turkey bones in Karnes's dishes and pots. Atmosphere: Open contempt, the witness's horror. Stakes: The conflict between commercial craft and the community's ideal of rawness.

After a dull session, Hilda takes Rumaker aside, confidentially asks him how to revive the class, then before he can answer exclaims that she will serve tea; the next time, a hot plate from Black Dwarf, tea bags, lemon, and cups from the kitchen; Virginia falls asleep within the first half hour, as always Words: Hilda: “Tea! Yes! I'll serve tea! That should liven things up!” Atmosphere: A pleasant break, a dazed class, three hours too long Stakes: The expected failure of Hilda's teaching

In the early winter darkness of 1952, with so few people at the college, walking into the dining hall for supper and hearing Bach played in just intonation on recorders by three musicians was a gentle clarity of spirit. Three recorders, Bach, winter darkness

Late on a cold December night, Rumaker heads for the Studies Building to write and finds Merrill standing by the road in front of it, with the odd impression that he was waiting for him. His pasty complexion even paler in the night, a crooked, hesitant smile, but a cold blue gaze of firm resolve. He comes straight to the point: does Rumaker want to sleep with him? Shaken (his first proposition at the college, from someone he has barely spoken to, and the image of Herb comes back to him), Rumaker mumbles that he will think about it, then repeats it louder, as he learned to do with his deaf brother. Merrill presses him to say when he will know, his head tilted to listen; then, very sure of himself, he says he will ask again in a few days. Rumaker flees to his studio on the lower floor of the Studies Building and locks the door. The dim light of the Studies entrance, visible breath, one of the college's 600 acres with no escape Consequences: Rumaker spends the following days on edge, watching for Merrill to appear

One evening, leaving the dining hall after his dishes, glad of the clear cold air after the steamy kitchen, Rumaker finds Merrill waiting for him in the shadows. In his soft but firm voice, Merrill asks for his answer. They walk side by side in the night, sizing each other up, past the Quiet House in its grotto of winter leaves, the stream by the print shop, the houses of Mrs. Jalowetz and of Victor Sprague and his wife, Minimum House, where the road turns right toward Next-to-the-Last-Chance. Rumaker decides to hell with it and goes on with him. Consequences: Leads to their first night together

Rumaker follows Merrill into the spartan front room, like an army barracks, heated by an army-surplus oil stove against a plasterboard wall; a light had been left on. Merrill offers him green tea, which he makes on a hot plate in the alcove kitchen; Rumaker has never tasted it and dares not ask what it is. Once the cup is empty and put in the sink, Merrill puts his hands on his shoulders and looks him in the eyes; it is too cold in the bedroom, kept closed to save heat, so he drags a single mattress out of it; Rumaker glimpses an enormous mattress taking up almost the whole floor, the marriage bed with Herb that he wonders whether Merrill keeps sacrosanct. Merrill slowly undresses him, examines him, lays him on the bare mattress, then undresses himself: a worn plaid flannel shirt, a T-shirt, jeans; a thin, muscular body, milky skin, chest and legs dusted with the same sandy brown as his crew cut. Green tea popularized at BMC by Cynthia Homire, an army oil stove, a hot plate, a single mattress versus a giant one, a glaring bulb, the cold floor despite the stove Consequences: Rumaker's first sexual relationship at the college, in the turmoil of guilt toward Herb

One evening at supper, during Rumaker's first winter, Roadside burns down. Wes Huss, whose turn it was to tend the furnace, is said to have left the damper or the door open (or both) before going down to eat. With no hoses, hydrants, or firefighting equipment on campus, everyone rushes out of the dining hall and watches the creosoted shingle building go up in a ball of flame, sparks on the pines, an orange glow; fears for Meadows Inn and Streamside. The volunteer firemen from Swannanoa and Black Mountain, miles away down the valley, arrive too late and stand by helplessly in their asbestos suits. Natasha goes by, leading her tiny mother, Madame Goldowski, who mutters “Dépêchons!”. The Husses and the Fiores lose everything, including recent wedding presents and a batch of Mary's new clothes. A building of creosoted wooden shingles; the firemen's asbestos suits; no hydrant or pumper. Consequences: An immediate rumor that Wes is to blame; losses made worse by the college's financial problems.

After the fire, Olson appears in the dormitory for the first time, ducks his big head under the door, and goes from one to another in a low, urgent voice: Wes is in bad shape, and whiskey would calm him. Rumaker, the only one with a bottle (a fifth of County Fair bourbon, the cheapest in the state according to Dan Rice, bought in Asheville a few days earlier and hidden under his underwear), says nothing, gnawed by a confused guilt but glad to keep his bottle, a silence that will haunt him for a long time. A bottle hidden at the back of a drawer, under the underwear, meant for Saturday nights. Consequences: Olson leaves empty-handed; Rumaker keeps a lasting sense of guilt.

Rosenberg defines the aesthetic foundation of Abstract Expressionism and christens it “Action Painting.” Pollock will claim that the term came from him (a conversation on a train from Manhattan). The article plants Rosenberg's flag on critical territory, lambastes his rival Greenberg, elevates de Kooning, and belittles Pollock. The famous quotation: the canvas as an “arena in which to act”; what goes on it is not a picture but an event Consequences: Contributes to Bill's apotheosis, along with Hess's article describing him at work in his studio
Death of Perdekamp, Albers's longtime correspondent Consequences: End of the correspondence

They cross the Atlas Mountains and the Sahara to Marrakech, then settle in Tangier around mid-December; Twombly does archaeology at the Roman ruins while Rauschenberg photographs the local tombstones (in a way reminiscent of Charles Olson's fascination with glyphs), a carnival (probably in Tetouan), and Twombly bathing under a rock in the arid landscape Tombstones, the carnival in Tetouan, bathing under a rock

Rosenberg formulates the figure of the action painter in ARTnews, echoing de Kooning's remarks at MoMA; Hess publishes the essay and will later play down his role. The essay names no painter, for theoretical reasons Consequences: The romantic image of the inspired artist takes hold

Merrill waits in the cold night, a crooked smile, resolve in his blue eyes; he asks without preamble whether Rumaker wants to sleep with him; Rumaker mumbles that he will think about it, then repeats it louder in the way he learned with his deaf brother; Merrill promises to ask again in a few days Words: Merrill asks for an answer, and says he will ask again in a few days Atmosphere: Visible breath, a pallid complexion, wounded pride beneath the coldness Stakes: The first sexual proposition received at BMC; guilt toward Herb

After the dishes, Merrill emerges from the shadows asking for his answer; they walk, sizing each other up, past the Quiet House, the print shop stream, the Jalowetz and Sprague houses, Minimum House; in the front room heated by the army stove, Merrill makes green tea on the hot plate (Rumaker's first cup), then puts his hands on his shoulders, drags a single mattress out of the bedroom with the big bed, slowly undresses him, and examines him under the glaring light before undressing in turn Words: “Like some green tea?”; “It'll be warmer here” Atmosphere: A heart pounding fit to burst, shame at not having showered, the cold floor despite the stove, harsh light Stakes: Surrender to desire, a transgression of Merrill and Herb's marriage bed

During supper, the cottage bursts into flames; everyone rushes out of the dining hall but stands helpless; sparks threaten the pines and the neighboring roofs; Natasha leads her tiny mother across the roots; the volunteer firemen arrive too late and look on in their asbestos suits; Wes, tall and gaunt, his face struck by the glow, is comforted by Olson's hand on his stooped shoulder, Bea and the baby beside him. Words: Madame Goldowski: “Dépêchons! Dépêchons!” Atmosphere: A ball of flame, smoke, sparks, a furious orange glow in the night, fear for the neighboring roofs. Stakes: Wes's fault, whispered as common knowledge, breaks a man before everyone's eyes.

Olson appears in the dormitory for the first time, ducks his big head under the door, and goes from bed to bed in a low, urgent voice asking for whiskey; Rumaker, the only one with a hidden bottle, says nothing, frozen by a confused guilt; Olson leaves empty-handed, somber and worried. Words: Olson: Wes is in a sorry state; does anyone have whiskey? It might calm him. Atmosphere: An evening of disaster, a low voice, Rumaker's guilty silence. Stakes: The narrator's secret selfishness against the simple generosity he thought himself capable of, a gesture that will haunt him.

In her mid-thirties, Elaine rents her first studio entirely her own, a walk-up she finds far too expensive, sleeping for the time being in the studio of her brother Peter, who has left for Europe; Bill's modest offer to pay a carpenter for racks and an easel swells into benches, a nightstand, a large table with metal legs, and pivoting partitions behind which one could imagine Sarah Bernhardt about to go onstage; her brother Conrad builds her bed; she compares her place to Bill's new studio (a skylight, linoleum waxed like a skating rink, a Murphy bed recalling Robin Hood's drawbridge with Douglas Fairbanks). Two benches four and a half feet long; pivoting partitions that Elaine calls a practical extension of the wall space

Income of $6,664.26, nearly all from sales of Bill's work at Sidney Janis ($6,202.76); Elaine earns little from her articles, a studio sale of drawings, and a juror's fee in Chicago; her expenses exceed her earnings ($350 in travel for lectures, juries, interviews); among her charitable donations, $100 to Catholic charities, although she says she stopped being Catholic at sixteen. Consequences: A pattern of debt she will repeat all her life

For ARTnews she reviews Nus d'Autrefois 1850-1900 (old pornographic photographs) and The Female Form in Painting; she writes that the photographers, freed from mythological or biblical disguise (Venus, Eve), present each woman as a specific individual, absent-mindedly erotic, funny, domestic, not at all remote, extravagantly recognizable images of the Second Sex, a sign that she knows Beauvoir (whose English translation appeared that year). An example of a classic photograph: bare breasts resting on a tray of apples; the author judges that these benevolent remarks do not amount to a recognizably feminist point of view
In 1953, a teaching invitation for Josef lets the couple discover Chile and Peru; they accept enthusiastically. Consequences: A decisive encounter with Andean textiles

Albers gives a Curso Preliminar at the PUC School of Architecture, developed through an American filter (Black Mountain, Yale) ranging from pedagogical reform and abstract art to studies of visual perception and color. Consequences: Influences the creation and outlook of the PUC Schools of Art and Design.

Even before his arrival, Albers asks that a large quantity of colored papers, as varied as possible and taken from everyday use, be collected. In Chile: exercises in making different colors look alike, or in drawing two different colors out of a single color by changing the ground. Colored papers from everyday use

Albers photographs many Peruvian sites and mounts the contact prints on board: Tampu Macchay at Sacsayhuamán, Pachacamac, Chan Chan (several montages, including a carved wall), Machu Picchu, Pisac. Each montage: 10 x ~8 inches (25.4 x ~20.3 cm) on board

A teaching invitation addressed to Josef allows the couple to travel to Chile and Peru, which they eagerly accept. Consequences: A logical sequel to their travels, up to the museum in Lima in August 1953
A milestone in Chilean art's abandonment of figuration in favor of abstraction, coinciding with Albers's visit.

Three ceramists come for three weeks each: MacKenzie (the rhythms of throwing and trimming), Rhodes (glaze formulation, wheel forms, textures, hand-building), Voulkos (working the clay until it collapses). 3 weeks per ceramist

McGee later sees Rauschenberg's first solo show at Betty Parsons: the now-famous White Paintings, hung in symmetrical groups. Standing in the middle of the gallery, his mind goes back to the first day at BMC, when Bob had helped them unload the Ford. Symmetrical hanging

In the “decline”: the Alberses (Anni at least) gone, leaving balls of yarn, weavings, warps and wefts, perhaps Peruvian or Mexican textile or ceramic fragments; salaries barely above the price of a train ticket (many hitchhike); food runs short, and five minutes after the meal gong there is nothing left. The meal gong; five minutes late means no more food; remnants of Anni Albers's weaving

The favorite sport of the summer of 1953: poker, together with picking the lock of the refrigerated locker to find something to eat, sometimes a steak (or what passed for one); everyone disapproved except Olson (6 feet 7 inches), whose intense hunger excused him. Picking the lock of the cold-storage locker; dubious steaks; Olson stands 6 feet 7 inches (2.01 m)

Penn begins directing for television in 1953 with orthodox material handled in an orthodox way, then moves away from naturalistic forms and experiments with techniques since absorbed as those of the New Wave in film. Only ten years later did he realize what he owed to the summer of 1948. Consequences: The lesson of Cage and Cunningham (risk that, change this) fertilizes his work
In the summer of 1953, Karnes and Weinrib are on the official bill with friends of their own, including Daniel Rhodes of Alfred University.

Black Mountain's last summer session: Vicente comes to teach painting, Tudor returns (he played Beethoven rather than scales to warm up his fingers, and people slipped into the dining hall to listen), Cunningham returns without Cage but with his company of seven dancers: Carolyn Brown, Viola Farber, Marianne Preger (Simon), Anita Dencks, Jo Anne Melsher (later killed in an accident), Remy Charlip, and Paul Taylor. Seven named dancers; Beethoven instead of scales Consequences: Cunningham calls that summer “a great big year for me — for us”.

Knowing the college had no money to pay his seven dancers, Cunningham asked only that they be given room and board, and himself gave up any salary. It was his first chance to work with them together, every day, in a sustained way: classes in the morning, rehearsals in the afternoon. Classes in the morning, rehearsals in the afternoon; no salary Consequences: The nucleus of the future Cunningham company is formed.

The Humphrey-Weidman and Martha Graham companies (and their offshoots, such as José Limón) dominated dance; Cunningham, with his chance-based, antic, nonnarrative methods, stood against them, a dominance he described in 1967 as “psychology — now it seems to be melodrama”. He could work as a soloist but had nowhere to take a coherent company. Consequences: Black Mountain's welcome in 1953 becomes decisive for the birth of his company.

After two weeks, Dencks came down with mumps; Cunningham replaced her with beginners who had come for the summer, including Harvey Lichtenstein (future director of the Brooklyn Academy of Music) and James Leo Herlihy, temporarily back, the owner of (and much embarrassed by) the biggest pair of feet Cunningham had ever seen. Mumps after two weeks

Farber had the impression that everyone knew everything, things she had never heard of; Charlip understood nothing of the poets' talk about the horizontal and the vertical, nor of Kline's painting class (architecture, negative space). But Charlip also remembers the beauty of seeing people live in relation to what they do, usually so separate; Farber, back from vacation, went to have a cup of tea in the kitchen and felt she was back home. A cup of tea in the kitchen

Cunningham had only the dining hall as a space, but the floor (as Litz had also found) was wonderful for dancing and the room entirely clear, with no fixed seats or fixed set. The physical conditions were not so wonderful, but the freedoms in what they had were wonderful.

In six weeks: four new dances (“Septet,” “Banjo,” “Dime a Dance,” “Untitled Solo”) and three performances for the community. An exhausting pace: dancing in the morning, rehearsal in the afternoon, meals, a nap, rehearsal in the evening, bed, to the point of knowing nothing about the rest of the summer. Six weeks, four dances, three performances Consequences: A warm reaction: “the school being very excited, the students being amazed and interested”; the nondancers had no idea what they were doing, a wonderful excitement.

At an earlier meeting in New York, Cunningham heard Tudor play nineteenth-century American composers; he was especially enchanted by Louis Gottschalk's “Banjo” and decided to use it at Black Mountain. Fourth Street apartment Consequences: Creation of the piece “Banjo” in the summer of 1953.

The regular pianist for the dance classes lacked the virtuosity for “Banjo”; the dancers did not like the piece. Tudor, busy preparing a concert of Wolpe's music, was persuaded to come and play for the dancers, “because they don't know what I'm doing... I don't know myself,” Cunningham told him. Tudor played, and it sounded like forty-five banjos at once; it was electric, fantastic. Forty-five banjos Consequences: The dancers finally understand the piece.

The hardest piece of the summer: Tudor worked on it with him every day, to music by Christian Wolff; physically and musically arduous, it made Cunningham give up in despair. One day he collapsed on the floor as if to say he was giving up; Tudor smiled at him and said: “Well, it's clearly impossible. But we're going right ahead and do it anyway.” And they did it, along with “Suite by Chance” (sound by Wolff), premiered earlier that year at the University of Illinois. Music by Christian Wolff

The bulls terrified the city students, hence poor care; a cow died, and so many others got mastitis that they were handed over to a local farmer; the remaining Hereford herd began, according to one student, to drown in its own shit, hence a big cleanup of the barns; during it the herd broke out through the fences, and Olson, with almost the whole community, ran through the pastures mooing to round it up. It was decided to sell. Mastitis, broken fences, mooing Consequences: The herd is sold.

The college first tried to play two bidders from rival mountain families against each other (neither was interested; both arrived armed to inspect the herd, which could have turned violent); the herd was then sold at auction just as the market price collapsed. Two armed bidders, coinciding with the drop in prices Consequences: Financial loss.

Williams took a separate mortgage on the farm of up to $25,000; large vegetable gardens planted (okra briefly considered the solution), a tobacco barn built for a cash crop; Len Billing, a former student of the 1930s, came back to supervise a reorganized work program; nine special work scholarships allowing up to thirty hours of labor a week. The kibbutz spirit was raging. $25,000 mortgage, okra, tobacco barn, nine scholarships, 30 hours a week

The scholarship holders lacked time to study and judged the distinctions between students contrary to the college's philosophy; others did not sign up for chores or did not show up (especially after Olson's classes, which ran into the small hours). The tobacco crop “didn't turn out too well” (Billing); Jack Rice (Dan's brother), who brought periodic order to the crews, resigned after a quarrel with Huss; in fact he had quarreled with almost everyone and exempted only Olson from incompetence and scheming. Consequences: The end of the kibbutz spirit.

In the sporadic search for an outsider combining access to funds with indifference to power, Wolpe, put in touch by the pianist Irma Jurist, meets Schram, a young graduate with no experience at all in school administration. Schram agrees to come and visit the college, spends two pleasant days there, won over by Olson's monumental presence and everyone's commitment, but declines. Schram: “I guess they were seizing at straws”; he compares the college to “a company convent” Consequences: Nothing; the search for an outside administrator fails.

The low point: a fire destroys the Roadside building; the longtime cook Malrey Few, along with Flola Shepard and Len Billing (who had tried to bring order to the chaos of the work program), resign; the expiration of GI Bill benefits threatens the loss of still more students. Consequences: At the end of 1953, the college is on the verge of closing: enrollment down to about two dozen students, no cash salary paid to the teachers for months.

Johanna Jalowetz reluctantly decides to move closer to her daughters, given her own growing frailty and the college's. She delays her departure while trying to sell part of Jalo's collection of books and manuscripts, including original Schoenberg scores, which brings her money only late and usually just enough to cover her moving expenses. Original Schoenberg scores, now enormously valuable, then sold off cheaply Consequences: The loss of a beloved figure from the early days.

After Rumaker's first year, the work scholarships are abolished, allowing him to concentrate on writing; he stays at the college, on and off, for three more years. Consequences: Rumaker can devote himself to writing.

A young English couple persuades the Creeleys to move to Majorca and set up a publishing house together, the Roebuck Press; the project soon fails, Creeley and Seymour-Smith not sharing the same interests. Consequences: The Creeleys carry on alone, under the name Divers Press.

At the end of 1953, the faculty accepts Creeley as editor, understanding that he would come to the college shortly; he had been invited as early as 1952 (announced in the official brochure for the 1952 summer session for a writing course). Low printing costs in Majorca: the magazine will be printed there throughout its life, even after Creeley's arrival. The printer Mossen Alcovar, unable to read English, setting it letter by letter. Consequences: Creeley's letter to Trocchi: “the job at Black Mountain finally came thru”.

At the end of 1953, about 25 students; the community thinks it can become self-supporting at 35, even though the year before, with 35 students, it had not been. The official 1952-1953 catalog had been vaguely dishonest and a promotional failure. 25 students; goal of 35. Consequences: The motivation for the magazine as a publicity tool.
